Chapter 9: Intentional Living—Choosing What Matters
After some time spent in solitude, surrounded by the quiet simplicity of the sea, the idea of intentional living really starts to mean something deeper. It’s not about following somebody else’s playbook, or chasing after what everyone else calls important.
It’s about making your choices—deciding how to spend your time, where you want to put your energy, what’s worth holding onto, and what you’re finally ready to let go.
Imagine standing at a crossroads, faced with a real decision. The old habit might be to rush, to pick whatever feels easiest, or to act out of fear. But now? There’s a pause. A moment to check in and ask yourself: Does this really line up with what matters most to me? Is this choice actually nourishing, or does it just leave me feeling drained?
Most people hardly ever stop to ask questions like that. Life moves fast, and it’s so easy to just get swept along. But the lessons from the sea? They encourage us to slow down and do things differently. There’s a new comfort in saying no to what doesn’t fit, and in making space for what truly does.
Living intentionally isn’t about getting everything perfect. It’s about actually paying attention. It’s noticing when life feels a little out of balance, and then making those small, gentle adjustments. It’s choosing to show up and be present, rather than getting lost in distractions. It’s reaching for depth instead of settling for the surface, and finding meaning in the middle of all the noise.
So, what happens when you start living like this? A lot of people find a real sense of freedom. The urge to always keep up, to compare, to compete—it starts to fade away. Suddenly, there’s more room for creativity, for real connection, and for simple joy. The days don’t feel so crowded. Your mind feels a little lighter.
Of course, intentional living isn’t a finish line. It’s a practice—something you come back to, again and again. There will be days when those old habits sneak in, when the world’s noise gets loud. But the memory of the sea, and that quiet cottage, is like a gentle reminder: You can always begin again.
